passage: Monday. Jasleen hummed the theme of her favourite dragon-baker cartoon at lunch. Yash grinned. "That is for babies!" Three boys laughed; Meera looked at her tiffin and said nothing. Wednesday. Yash asked who still watched it. "Not me," said Jasleen. "I stopped ages ago." The laughing moved on to someone else, and her shoulders dropped. Saturday. At home she watched the new episode with the volume low, one ear on the door. The dragon burned the bread again. She smiled, then felt a small pinch, as if she had left something outside in the rain.

qa.q: What did Jasleen say when Yash asked who still watched the cartoon?
qa.a: Jasleen said "Not me" and claimed she had stopped ages ago.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Jasleen have on Wednesday and on Saturday?
qa.a: Relief when the laughing moves on, and a small pinch of having betrayed something she loves, like leaving a favourite thing out in the rain.

qa.q: What choice could help Jasleen enjoy the cartoon without being mocked?
qa.a: Jasleen could quietly tell Meera, who said nothing, that it is still a favourite; one person who knows makes the taste feel less like a secret.

qa.q: How might Meera feel as the boys laugh at Jasleen?
qa.a: Meera may feel uneasy; looking at her tiffin and saying nothing suggests she does not want to join in but also does not want to be the next target.

grounding: A child stops admitting a liked cartoon after others mock it, feeling relief at not standing out and a small betrayal of self.

passage: Sit, beta, and let your Nani tell you something silly. I was ten, and in those days everyone called me Vinita. I loved humming an old radio song about a boatman. Then our class laughed at it. Jahnavi, the loudest girl, called it a grandmother's song, and the others giggled while one boy stared at his desk. After that I told everyone I liked the new film songs. I felt light, as if I had put down a heavy bag. But every evening I hummed the boatman song into my pillow. Years later Jahnavi told me she had known every word of it too.

qa.q: Which song did Vinita hum before the class laughed?
qa.a: Vinita hummed an old radio song about a boatman.

qa.q: Why did Vinita say she liked the new film songs instead?
qa.a: Vinita wanted the laughing to stop; the relief was like putting down a heavy bag, though Vinita went on humming the boatman song into the pillow, so a small loss stayed behind.

qa.q: What small step could have let Vinita keep the song without being mocked?
qa.a: Vinita could have hummed it near one kind listener, or said calmly that it was a favourite whatever the others thought.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi have felt when calling the song a grandmother's song while knowing every word of it?
qa.a: Jahnavi probably felt the same pull to fit in, hiding a real liking behind a joke, which shows other children may be hiding private tastes too.

grounding: A child hides a liked song once others mock it, feeling relief at not standing out and a private sense of betraying oneself.

passage:
On the school bus from Sonpur, the back seats started on the buffalo cartoon. “My cousin watches it,” Parul said. “She is three.” Everyone laughed. Sonali laughed too, a little late.
“Sonali, you watched it last week, na?” asked Bhola.
“Me? No. Only my little brother,” she said, looking out at the mustard fields.
That evening the cartoon played on the old television in the courtyard. Her brother patted the mat. Sonali sat, then shifted so her back was to the gate. When the buffalo sang, she mouthed every word, quietly, and felt a pinch she could not name.

qa.q: Who did Parul say watches the buffalo cartoon?
qa.a: Parul said a cousin who is three watches it.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling when she mouthed the song with her back to the gate?
qa.a: She felt torn: relieved nobody from the bus could see, but a little guilty and sad about denying something she loves.

qa.q: What would you advise Sonali about the bus conversation next time?
qa.a: She could say lightly that she still enjoys it, or simply stay quiet, without having to deny it; finding one friend who likes it too would help.

qa.q: How might Sonali's little brother see her watching?
qa.a: He probably just sees his sister sitting with him to enjoy the show and has no idea she denied it that morning.

grounding: Shows a child who denies liking a cartoon once classmates mock it, relieved but quietly uneasy about it.

passage:
Pablo's grandfather had played the accordion tune every Sunday in their flat in Valencia, and Pablo kept a recording of it on his old phone.
At lunch Omar grabbed one of his earphones. “What is this? Old-man music!” He held it up so Lucía and Marco could hear. They groaned and laughed.
“It's nothing. It was on shuffle,” Pablo said, and pulled the earphone back.
“Shuffle from 1950,” Marco said.
Pablo switched to a pop song everyone knew and nodded along. His shoulders dropped. Later, walking home alone, he played the accordion recording twice, turned down very low.

qa.q: What did Omar call the music?
qa.a: Omar called it old-man music.

qa.q: How can you tell Pablo felt relieved after switching songs, yet uneasy?
qa.a: His shoulders dropped once he played the pop song, showing relief, but he played the accordion recording twice later alone, which shows a quiet guilt about denying it.

qa.q: What could Pablo try if it happens again?
qa.a: He could say something simple like "It's my grandfather's tune, I like it" and move on, which often ends teasing faster than hiding.

qa.q: What might Omar not realise about the song?
qa.a: Omar probably doesn't know it is linked to Pablo's grandfather's Sundays, so he doesn't see the joke touches something personal.

grounding: Shows a child denying a song he loves once classmates mock it, gaining relief at the cost of a small self-betrayal.

passage:
Lights-out was at nine in the Class 6 girls' dormitory. Keerthana had the rabbit cartoon paused on the shared tablet during free time.
Aditi leaned over. “Pink rabbit? Seriously?” Two other girls on the next bunk giggled. “My sister stopped that in Class 2.”
Keerthana's ears went hot. “It came on by itself,” she said, and switched to a quiz video.
“Good,” Aditi said, flopping back. “I thought you were a baby.”
Everyone moved on to talking about the sports meet. Keerthana joined in, relieved. But when the matron switched off the lights, she lay hugging her pillow, humming the rabbit's song under her breath where nobody could hear.

qa.q: What did Keerthana switch to?
qa.a: She switched to a quiz video.

qa.q: What does Keerthana humming the song in the dark suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: It suggests she still loves the cartoon and feels a little sad and guilty for pretending otherwise, even though she was relieved in the moment.

qa.q: How could a matron or teacher make the dorm safer for different tastes?
qa.a: They could make free-time choices a normal mix, for example letting each girl pick a show in turn, so nobody is mocked for liking something younger.

qa.q: How does Aditi seem to see the moment?
qa.a: For Aditi it was a quick joke; she moved on at once and doesn't notice how much it cost Keerthana.

grounding: Shows a child in a hostel hiding that she likes a cartoon after roommates laugh, relieved but privately betraying herself.

passage: Monday: Harish came to school humming the song from Chotu the Elephant, his favourite cartoon. Sonali laughed. 'That's for babies!' The boys around her laughed too. Harish went red and stopped humming. Wednesday: when Mohan asked what everyone watched after school, Harish said, 'Cricket highlights,' and the others nodded. It felt good not to be laughed at, and also a bit like lying to himself. Saturday: at home, Harish watched Chotu the Elephant with the sound low, so nobody passing the window would hear. His little sister sang along loudly. He almost told her to stop, then quietly hummed with her.

qa.q: What did Harish say he watched after school?
qa.a: Cricket highlights.

qa.q: How did Harish feel after giving the cricket answer?
qa.a: Relieved not to be laughed at, but also a little guilty, as if lying to himself.

qa.q: What small step could help Harish keep his own taste?
qa.a: Share it with one friend who might like it too, and remember that liking a cartoon isn't babyish.

qa.q: How might Sonali see her 'That's for babies!' comment?
qa.a: She may think it was a harmless joke, not realising it made Harish hide something he loved.

grounding: Over a week a child stops admitting he likes a cartoon after classmates mock it, feeling relief and a small self-betrayal.
